title: Copying Rows and Upserts
summary: Insert rows from a query, skip duplicates, and update rows that already exist.
intro: Real data rarely arrives one row at a time. A delivery, an import, or a nightly sync brings a whole batch, and some of it is new while some of it is already in your table. This lesson copies rows with a query and decides what happens when a key already exists.

steps.title: Copying rows with INSERT SELECT
steps.body:
This lesson uses two tables. `inventory` holds what a shop has in stock, one row per `sku` (stock code). `shipment` is a delivery that just arrived:

```sql
CREATE TABLE inventory (sku text PRIMARY KEY, name text, qty integer);
CREATE TABLE shipment (sku text, name text, qty integer);
```

| table | rows (sku, name, qty) |
| --- | --- |
| inventory | A100 Desk lamp 12, B200 Office chair 5, C300 Notebook 40, D400 Stapler 8 |
| shipment | B200 Office chair 3, D400 Heavy stapler 15, E500 Monitor stand 6, F600 Desk mat 20 |

So far `INSERT` took rows from `VALUES`. Put a `SELECT` in its place and every row the query returns is inserted:

```sql
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, name, qty)
SELECT sku, name, qty FROM shipment WHERE qty > 5;
```

The query can use `WHERE`, joins, expressions, anything a normal `SELECT` can. Its columns fill the listed columns **by position**, not by name, so keep both lists in the same order. The tag `INSERT 0 n` tells you how many rows were copied, and it is `INSERT 0 0` when the query finds nothing.

example.title: Stocking the new items
example.prompt: Copy only the shipment rows whose sku is not in inventory yet, then list inventory.
example.output:
INSERT 0 2

 sku  |     name      | qty
------+---------------+-----
 A100 | Desk lamp     |  12
 B200 | Office chair  |   5
 C300 | Notebook      |  40
 D400 | Stapler       |   8
 E500 | Monitor stand |   6
 F600 | Desk mat      |  20
(6 rows)
example.explanation: `SELECT sku FROM inventory` lists the four skus already in stock, so `NOT IN` keeps only E500 and F600 from the shipment. Those two rows go into `inventory`, and the tag says `INSERT 0 2`. B200 and D400 are skipped, so their quantities stay 5 and 8. `NOT IN` is safe here because `sku` is the primary key, so the list never holds a NULL.

practice.title: Copying the big deliveries
practice.prompt:
Copy the large lines of the shipment into a new table.

1. Create a table `big_items` with columns `sku text PRIMARY KEY`, `name text`, and `qty integer`.
2. Insert into `big_items` the `sku`, `name`, and `qty` of every `shipment` row with `qty` over 10, using `INSERT ... SELECT`.
3. List every column of `big_items`, sorted by `sku`.

Expected output:

```text
CREATE TABLE

INSERT 0 2

 sku  |     name      | qty
------+---------------+-----
 D400 | Heavy stapler |  15
 F600 | Desk mat      |  20
(2 rows)
```

hints: Write `CREATE TABLE big_items (...)` first, so the insert has somewhere to go.
Use `INSERT INTO big_items (sku, name, qty)` followed by a `SELECT ... FROM shipment WHERE qty > 10`.
When no row matches, the tag is `INSERT 0 0` and the list shows `(0 rows)`.

steps.title: Skipping duplicates with DO NOTHING
steps.body:
`inventory.sku` is the primary key, so copying the whole `shipment` (which has B200 and D400 again) stops at the first repeat:

```text
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint "inventory_pkey"
```

The whole statement fails, so not even the new rows are added. Add `ON CONFLICT (column) DO NOTHING` and each row that would break the key is skipped quietly while the rest go in:

```sql
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, name, qty)
VALUES ('B200', 'Office chair', 1)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO NOTHING;
```

The column in parentheses must have a `UNIQUE` or `PRIMARY KEY` constraint, because that is how PostgreSQL finds the clash. On a plain column you get:

```text
ERROR:  there is no unique or exclusion constraint matching the ON CONFLICT specification
```

An identity id never clashes, because PostgreSQL picks a new one each time. So upserts match on a natural key, like `sku` or an email. Leave out `(sku)` and `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` skips a clash on any unique column. The tag counts only rows actually written: the statement above prints `INSERT 0 0`. Try both errors in the editor: remove the `ON CONFLICT` line, or insert into `shipment` instead, which has no key.

example.title: Adding the shipment once
example.prompt: Insert every shipment row into inventory, skipping skus it already has, then list inventory.
example.output:
INSERT 0 2

 sku  |     name      | qty
------+---------------+-----
 A100 | Desk lamp     |  12
 B200 | Office chair  |   5
 C300 | Notebook      |  40
 D400 | Stapler       |   8
 E500 | Monitor stand |   6
 F600 | Desk mat      |  20
(6 rows)
example.explanation: All four shipment rows are tried. B200 and D400 clash with the primary key, so `DO NOTHING` skips them and the tag reads `INSERT 0 2`, not 4. The skipped rows change nothing: D400 keeps the name Stapler and qty 8. Unlike `NOT IN`, the check happens inside the insert, so you do not need a subquery.

The conflict clause goes after the last row and before the semicolon: `ON CONFLICT (sku) DO NOTHING;`.

steps.title: Upserts with DO UPDATE
steps.body:
An **upsert** inserts a row, or updates it if the key already exists. Swap `DO NOTHING` for `DO UPDATE SET`:

```sql
INSERT INTO inventory (sku, name, qty)
VALUES ('B200', 'Office chair', 3)
ON CONFLICT (sku) DO UPDATE SET qty = inventory.qty + EXCLUDED.qty;
```

Inside `SET` you can see two rows:

- `inventory.qty` is the row already in the table.
- `EXCLUDED.qty` is the row you tried to insert.

Write the table name on the existing value. A bare `qty` fails with `column reference "qty" is ambiguous`, because both rows have it. `SET` takes several columns separated by commas, just like `UPDATE`. Unlike `DO NOTHING`, `DO UPDATE` always needs the `(sku)` part, so PostgreSQL knows which key to match.

The tag counts inserted and updated rows together, so the statement above prints `INSERT 0 1`. One gotcha: if the same sku appears twice in one insert, PostgreSQL refuses to update a row twice:

```text
ERROR:  ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE command cannot affect row a second time
```

Why upsert at all? It replaces a check, then an insert or update, with one statement that cannot be split by another session in between.

example.title: Adding stock to the shelves
example.prompt: Add the whole shipment to inventory: insert new skus and add the quantity to skus already in stock.
example.output:
INSERT 0 4

 sku  |     name      | qty
------+---------------+-----
 A100 | Desk lamp     |  12
 B200 | Office chair  |   8
 C300 | Notebook      |  40
 D400 | Stapler       |  23
 E500 | Monitor stand |   6
 F600 | Desk mat      |  20
(6 rows)
example.explanation: E500 and F600 are new, so they are inserted as they are. B200 and D400 clash, so their existing rows are updated: `inventory.qty + EXCLUDED.qty` gives 5 + 3 = 8 and 8 + 15 = 23. Only `qty` is in `SET`, so D400 keeps its old name. Two inserts and two updates make `INSERT 0 4`.

recap:
- `INSERT INTO t (cols) SELECT ...` inserts every row the query returns, matching columns by position.
- `ON CONFLICT (col) DO NOTHING` skips rows whose key already exists.
- The conflict column needs a `UNIQUE` or `PRIMARY KEY` constraint.
- `INSERT 0 n` counts only rows written, inserted or updated.
- `ON CONFLICT (col) DO UPDATE SET ...` turns a clash into an update.
- `EXCLUDED.col` is the value you tried to insert, `table.col` is the value already there.
